stop-procrastination-fast-5-minute-reset.title: Use a Five-Minute Start for an Avoided Task
stop-procrastination-fast-5-minute-reset.subtitle: Define one visible first action, begin briefly, then review the real obstacle
stop-procrastination-fast-5-minute-reset.description: When you notice that you are avoiding an important task, define one visible first action, work on it for five minutes, then decide whether to continue, revise the next step, or stop and resolve a blocker.
stop-procrastination-fast-5-minute-reset.reason: Replace an inherited procrastination article containing fabricated trials, percentages, causal mechanisms, universal timing claims and app promotion with a bounded task-initiation protocol that makes no effectiveness claim.

lifeOsSource.hack: Notice that you have drifted away from an important task, name one visible first action, and work only on that action for five minutes before deciding what comes next.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the smallest visible action that would count as beginning the task. Set a five-minute timer, do only that action, and stop when the timer ends long enough to decide whether to continue, make the step smaller, clarify the task, or remove a blocker.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I complete the first visible action? If not, was the step still too large, unclear, blocked by missing information, or not appropriate to do now?

faq.question: Does the start need to last exactly five minutes?
faq.answer: No. Five minutes is a convenient default, not an optimal dose. Use a shorter interval when the first action is tiny or a slightly longer one when setup itself takes time.

faq.question: What counts as a visible first action?
faq.answer: Choose an action with a clear end state: open the correct file and write the heading, list three required inputs, send one clarification question, or create the first empty structure for the work.

faq.question: What if I still cannot begin?
faq.answer: Do not keep shrinking the timer while leaving the obstacle unnamed. Check whether the task is unclear, too large, missing information, waiting on another person, lower priority than claimed, or something that should be paused rather than forced.

intro.html: Sometimes the hardest part of an important task is crossing the boundary between thinking about it and producing the first visible piece of work. This protocol creates a small, reversible start and a review point. It does not claim that five minutes solves procrastination or that continuing is always the right decision.

sections.title: 1. Notice the drift without diagnosing yourself
sections.html: When you realize that you are reorganizing, browsing, or doing unrelated work instead of the intended task, write a neutral observation: I have not started the report. Avoid turning one delayed start into a judgment about your character.

sections.title: 2. Define one visible first action
sections.html: Choose the smallest action that produces an observable change in the task. Good examples include opening the correct file and writing a heading, listing the inputs you need, drafting one question, or creating the first row of a table. Work on the report is still too vague.

sections.title: 3. Set a bounded start
sections.html: Set a five-minute timer and work only on the first action. The timer is permission to reassess, not a promise that you must stop or a claim that five minutes is special. Remove unrelated tabs and notifications only when they interfere with this specific start.

sections.title: 4. Begin without expanding the scope
sections.html: Complete the first action before adding new goals. If you discover missing information, record exactly what is missing. If the task is larger than expected, leave a visible continuation point instead of quietly converting the five-minute start into an undefined work session.

sections.title: 5. Review when the timer ends
sections.html: Choose deliberately among four outcomes: continue for another defined interval, make the next action smaller, clarify the task, or stop and resolve a blocker. Stopping with a clearer task is a valid result; drifting into unrelated work without recording why is not.

sections.title: 6. Do not use a small start to force the wrong work
sections.html: Pause when the task is unsafe, lacks required approval or information, conflicts with a more important commitment, or should reasonably be delegated or cancelled. A task-initiation protocol should expose those conditions, not help you ignore them more efficiently.
